Lab 10

Penguin

Build a penguin from spheres, give it a skeleton, and make it wave in Blender.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how animators build a character from simple shapes, give it a skeleton, and bring it to life with keyframes.

You need Blender 4.2 or newer, a mouse with a scroll wheel (on a laptop trackpad, see this fix), and the two penguin drawings from Step 2. This lab takes about three lessons. Save your file as Lab10_Penguin_YourName.blend.

You’ve got it when you can

  • place reference drawings and line them up with the grid
  • build a character from spheres using exact Location, Rotation and Scale numbers
  • duplicate and mirror parts, and name objects properly
  • build a six-bone skeleton with extrude and Symmetrize
  • attach the body to the skeleton and explain parent and child
  • set keyframes in Pose Mode and play a looping wave

The plan

Six parts. Each one ends with a picture of what your penguin should look like.

  1. Part 1Set up the drawingsSteps 1–6
  2. Part 2Build the bodySteps 7–12
  3. Part 3Mirror, feet, namesSteps 13–15
  4. Part 4Build the skeletonSteps 16–22
  5. Part 5Attach the bodySteps 23–25
  6. Part 6Animate the waveSteps 26–31

Eggs, bones and keys

A character animator’s job has three layers. The model is the shape you see. The rig is a skeleton hidden inside it that gives you handles to move. The animation is a short list of poses at chosen moments, and the computer fills in the movement between them.

Your penguin is eight squashed spheres, six bones and five poses. Everything is built from exact numbers, so if yours matches the pictures at each checkpoint, the next part will work. If it doesn’t, the fix is almost always one number.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Reference image
A drawing placed in the 3D scene to trace over. It never renders.
Empty
An object with no shape. A reference image is a kind of Empty.
Orthographic view
A flat view with no perspective, so sizes can be compared. Front, Right and Top are orthographic.
UV Sphere
Blender’s basic ball, made of rings like a globe.
Sidebar
The panel that slides out on the right of the viewport when you press N. Its Item tab shows exact numbers.
Armature
A skeleton object. Its parts are bones.
Head and tail
The fat end and the thin tip of a bone. A bone pivots at its head.
Parent and child
A child follows its parent. Bones have parents; objects can too.
Extrude
Grow something new out of what is selected. With bones, E grows a child bone from a tip.
Symmetrize
Mirror the .L bones to make .R bones.
Pose Mode
The mode for bending a finished skeleton. Edit Mode changes the skeleton itself.
Automatic weights
Blender decides how strongly each bone pulls each part of the mesh, by distance.
Keyframe
A saved pose at one frame. Shown as a yellow diamond.
Interpolation
How Blender fills in between keyframes. Bezier (default) eases; Linear is constant speed.
Timeline
The strip at the bottom that shows frames, keyframes and the current-frame marker.

Part 1

Set up the drawings

Tools: Add › Image › Reference, the navigation gizmo and Wireframe shading.

A penguin is a stack of eggs. Before you make any eggs you put two drawings of the penguin into Blender, one seen from the front and one from the side, so that every sphere you add can be matched against them. The drawings cross each other like a + seen from above.

How the steps work

Each step has a Where line (which part of the Blender window to look at), a Watch animation of the mouse doing the step (pause it, drag the slider, or use the arrow buttons to go one move at a time), and a Do this list of the same moves as a, b, c. Do one move, look at the animation, do the next. The drawings are simplified, not screenshots: the words and positions match Blender, the exact colours and spacing may not.

  1. Start fresh and save

    Layout workspace › the File menu at the very top-left.

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › New › General. You get a cube, a camera and a light.
    2. b
      Click the cube once (orange outline), press X and click Delete. Keep the camera and the light.
    3. c
      File › Save As. Find your Lab 10 folder, type the name Lab10_Penguin_YourName and click Save Blender File.

    You should now see: the window title shows your file name, and the Outliner (top right) lists only Camera and Light.

    Why save first?

    Blender only auto-saves a file that already has a name. From now on press Ctrl+S every few steps; it takes a second and saves you a lesson.

  2. Get the two drawings

    Your Lab 10 folder (the same one the .blend is in).

    Download penguin_front.png Download penguin_side.png

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click both download buttons. Your browser puts the files in Downloads.
    2. b
      Move them into your Lab 10 folder, next to the .blend. (Blender remembers where its images live; if they move later the drawings go pink.)

    You should now see: two PNG files in the folder. Each is a square picture with a dotted line down the middle.

    Why two drawings?

    A front view tells you how wide and tall each egg is. Only a side view tells you how deep it is. The beak and the feet stick forward, which you cannot see from the front at all.

  3. Look at the penguin from the front

    The navigation gizmo: the coloured circles in the top-right corner of the 3D Viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the mouse over the viewport. Find the gizmo: a red X, green Y and blue Z circle, each with a hollow twin opposite it.
    2. b
      Click the hollow green circle (the one opposite Y; hover it and it says -Y). The view snaps and the top-left text reads Front Orthographic.
    3. c
      Keyboard way: Numpad 1. On a laptop with no numpad use the gizmo.

    You should now see: Front Orthographic written in the top-left of the viewport, and a flat grid with a red line (the X axis) and a green line.

    Why not press the X key?

    In Blender the X key means delete. The old version of this lab said “press -y” and “press X” for the views, and plenty of penguins vanished. Views are the gizmo or the numpad; letters are tools.

  4. Add the front drawing

    Add menu in the viewport header, then a file window.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Still in Front view. Hover the viewport and press Shift+C so the 3D cursor sits at the centre (new things appear at the cursor). Then click Add in the viewport header.
    2. b
      Hover Image, click Reference. A file window opens.
    3. c
      Find your Lab 10 folder, click penguin_front.png, click Add Image.
    4. d
      The drawing appears centred on the grid, 5 m square, with an orange outline (it is selected). Hover the viewport and press G then Z, type 1.45, press Enter. It rises 1.45 m.

    You should now see: the penguin standing on the green ground line, with the red centre line running down the middle of its body. In the Outliner a new Empty has appeared: that is the drawing.

    Why 1.45?

    Blender drops every reference image with its centre on the grid, so half of the penguin was underground. The drawing was made so that lifting it 1.45 m puts its feet exactly on the ground line. Every number in this lab assumes that.

  5. Turn to the side and add the side drawing

    The gizmo again, then the same Add menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the red X circle on the gizmo (or Numpad 3). The text reads Right Orthographic. The front drawing is now edge-on, so it looks like a line or disappears: that is correct.
    2. b
      Add › Image › Reference, click penguin_side.png, Add Image.
    3. c
      G Z 1.45 Enter: lift it the same 1.45 m.

    You should now see: the side penguin with its beak pointing LEFT, feet on the ground line. The Outliner now has Empty and Empty.001.

    Why does the beak point left?

    Right view looks at the penguin from its right side. The front of the penguin (the -Y direction) is then on the left of the screen. If your beak points right you added the wrong file: delete the Empty and redo the step.

  6. Orbit, then switch to wireframe

    The viewport, and the row of four shading circles at the top-right of its header.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hold the middle mouse button (press the wheel) and drag. The view orbits. You see the two drawings crossing at right angles. From most angles you only see half of each: normal.
    2. b
      Hover the viewport and press Shift+Z. The spheres you add next will be see-through wire, so the drawings show through them.
    3. c
      Click the -Y circle (or Numpad 1) to go back to Front view. Press Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: Front view, the front drawing face-on, and the second shading circle (hollow one) highlighted in the header.

    Why wireframe?

    In Solid shading every sphere is a grey blob that hides the drawing behind it. Wireframe draws only the edges, so you can line the sphere up with the pencil lines. Shift+Z toggles it back whenever you want to see the solid penguin.

End of Part 1. Save.

Part 2

Build the body from spheres

Tools: Add › Mesh › UV Sphere, G, S and the N sidebar.

Every part of the penguin is one UV Sphere, moved and squashed into an egg. You will place the first one by hand, then learn the exact way: typing numbers into the sidebar. Play with the sliders first to see what each number does.

Sphere lab: Location and Scale

One sphere over the two drawings. Drag the sliders and watch both views. Can you make it fit the belly?

  1. The first sphere, roughly

    Viewport header › Add menu. Front view, Wireframe on.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport, press Shift+C: the 3D cursor (the red-and-white ring) jumps to the centre. New objects appear wherever that cursor is.
    2. b
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. A 1 m ball appears at the centre, selected.
    3. c
      Press G then Z, move the mouse up until the ball sits over the belly, click to drop it.
    4. d
      Press S, move the mouse towards or away from the ball until it is roughly belly-sized, click.

    You should now see: a wire ball roughly on the belly. Roughly is fine: the next step makes it exact.

    Why G Z and not just G?

    G alone moves the ball in any direction, which is hard to control. Pressing Z straight after G locks the move to the up-and-down axis. The same trick works for X and Y, and for R (rotate) and S (scale).

  2. Make it exact with the sidebar

    Press N over the viewport. The sidebar opens on the right edge of the viewport; use its Item tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport and press N. A panel slides out on the right with Location, Rotation and Scale. If it shows something else, click its Item tab.
    2. b
      Location: click the Z box, type 0.95, press Enter. X and Y stay 0.
    3. c
      Scale: click X, type 0.85, Enter. Then Y 0.75, then Z 0.85.
    4. d
      Compare: the wire egg should sit right on the belly outline. Press Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: the sphere fitting the belly in the drawing, and the sidebar reading Location 0, 0, 0.95 and Scale 0.85, 0.75, 0.85.

    Why type numbers at all?

    Everyone’s penguin then matches the drawing and, more importantly, the skeleton numbers in Part 4. A belly that is 10 cm off makes the bones miss it. Dragging is for getting close; typing is for getting it right.

    3. The next four parts are the same recipe: add a UV Sphere (or a Cone), then type the numbers. Here they all are. The steps below show each one.

    PartLoc XLoc YLoc ZRot XRot YRot ZScale XScale YScale Z
    Belly0 m0 m0.95 m0°0°0°0.850.750.85
    Chest0 m0 m1.75 m0°0°0°0.650.60.6
    Head0 m0 m2.45 m0°0°0°0.450.450.45
    Beak (Cone)0 m-0.45 m2.4 m90°0°0°0.120.120.3
    Arm.L0.95 m0 m1.55 m0°-25°0°0.180.30.75
    Arm.R-0.95 m0 m1.55 m0°25°0°0.180.30.75
    Foot.L0.35 m-0.15 m0.12 m0°0°0°0.280.450.12
    Foot.R-0.35 m-0.15 m0.12 m0°0°0°0.280.450.12

    Blue cells are the ones you type. Grey cells stay at their default.

  3. The chest

    Viewport header › Add, then the sidebar.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. The new ball appears at the 3D cursor, which is still at the centre: it is hiding inside the belly. That is fine.
    2. b
      Sidebar: Location Z 1.75. Scale X 0.65, Y 0.6, Z 0.6.

    You should now see: a smaller egg sitting on top of the belly, overlapping it a little, matching the chest outline.

    Why do the eggs overlap?

    Real penguins have no gaps. Overlapping spheres read as one smooth body once the material is on. The skeleton will bend the overlaps as if they were one shape.

  4. The head

    Same two places: Add, then the sidebar.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere.
    2. b
      Sidebar: Location Z 2.45. Scale X, Y and Z all 0.45.

    You should now see: a round head on top. Three eggs, standing in a line down the red centre line.

  5. The beak is a cone

    Add › Mesh › Cone, the sidebar, then the X circle on the gizmo to check.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cone (not a sphere).
    2. b
      Sidebar: Location Y -0.45, Z 2.4. Rotation X 90. Scale 0.12, 0.12, 0.3.
    3. c
      Click the red X circle on the gizmo (Right view). The beak must stick out to the LEFT of the head, like the drawing. Then click -Y to come back to Front view.

    You should now see: from the front, a small circle on the face; from the right, a pointed beak sticking forward.

    Why Rotation X 90?

    A new cone points straight up. Turning it 90° around the X axis lays it on its side so the point faces -Y, which is the front of the penguin. Location Y -0.45 then pushes it forward out of the head.

  6. The first flipper

    Add, then the sidebar. Watch the Rotation row this time.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere.
    2. b
      Sidebar: Location X 0.95, Z 1.55. Rotation Y -25. Scale X 0.18, Y 0.3, Z 0.75.
    3. c
      Press Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: a tall thin egg on the screen-right side of the body, its top tilted in toward the chest and its tip out. That is the penguin’s LEFT flipper (it is facing you).

    Why is left on the right?

    The penguin faces you, so its left is your right. Blender’s +X axis points to screen-right in Front view, and later the bone on this side will be called Arm.L. Keep that straight and Part 4 will make sense.

End of Part 2. Save.

Part 3

Mirror, feet and names

Tools: Shift+D (duplicate), R (rotate) and F2 (rename).

You never build the second flipper. You copy the first and flip it. Then two flat feet, and then every part gets a proper name, because in Part 4 you need to tell the bones and the body parts apart.

  1. Copy the flipper to the other side

    The viewport. Keep an eye on the sidebar to see the numbers change.

    Predict first: The copy starts tilted exactly like the original. Which way does it need to tilt to be a mirror image? Say it before you press R.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the flipper so it is the only thing selected (orange).
    2. b
      Press Shift+D. A copy appears exactly on top, stuck to your mouse. Do not move the mouse yet.
    3. c
      Press X, type -1.9, press Enter. The copy slides 1.9 m to the other side (0.95 − 1.9 = −0.95).
    4. d
      It leans the wrong way. Press R, Y, type 50, Enter. Now it mirrors the first flipper.

    You should now see: two flippers, a mirror image of each other. The sidebar for the copy reads Location X -0.95 and Rotation Y 25.

    Why 50 and not 25?

    The copy started at -25° like the original. Rotating by 50 takes it from -25 to +25: the same tilt the other way. The sidebar shows the result, 25°.

  2. Two flat feet

    Add, the sidebar, then Shift+D again.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. Sidebar: Location X 0.35, Y -0.15, Z 0.12. Scale X 0.28, Y 0.45, Z 0.12.
    2. b
      With the foot selected: Shift+D, then X, type -0.7, Enter. The copy slides to -0.35.
    3. c
      Check in Right view (red X circle): the feet stick forward, under the belly. Back to Front (-Y).

    You should now see: two flat eggs at the bottom, on the ground line, one each side of the centre line.

    Why Scale Y 0.45?

    Feet are long front-to-back and flat. Scale Y stretches the egg toward you and away from you, which you only see in the side view. Scale Z 0.12 squashes it flat.

  3. Name every part

    The viewport and the Outliner (top right). F2 renames whatever is active.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the big belly sphere. In the Outliner its row (currently Sphere) lights up.
    2. b
      Hover the viewport and press F2. A small box pops up with the old name selected. Type Belly and press Enter.
    3. c
      Do the same seven more times: Chest, Head, Beak, Arm.L (the screen-right flipper), Arm.R, Foot.L (screen-right), Foot.R. Capital letters and the dots matter.
    4. d
      Press Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: the Outliner listing the eight names below, plus Camera, Light and the two Empties.

    Why names now?

    In Part 5 you will select all eight parts in one go and the Outliner is the easiest place to check them. In Part 4 the bones get names like Arm.L too; a mesh called Sphere.004 next to a bone called Arm.L is how people lose track.

End of Part 3. Save. This is a good place to end a lesson.

Part 4

Build the skeleton

Tools: Add › Armature, Edit Mode, E (extrude), Symmetrize and Pose Mode.

A skeleton in Blender is called an armature. It is made of bones, and bones belong to a family: move a parent and its children come too. You will build six bones, exactly, with numbers, then test them by bending the skeleton.

Bone family tree

The six bones you are about to build. Drag a slider to bend one bone and watch who follows.

  1. Add the armature and make it show through

    Add menu, then the Properties editor (bottom right) › the green stick-figure tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Object Mode, Front view, Wireframe on. Hover the viewport and press Shift+C so the cursor is at the centre.
    2. b
      Add › Armature. A single bone appears standing on the centre point, 1 m tall, inside the belly. In the Outliner a new Armature appears.
    3. c
      In the Properties editor (bottom right, the column of icons) click the green stick-figure tab: Armature Data.
    4. d
      Click Viewport Display to open that panel, then tick In Front.

    You should now see: the bone drawn on top of the penguin. (In Wireframe you could see it anyway; In Front keeps it visible when you switch back to Solid.)

    Why In Front?

    The skeleton lives inside the body. Without In Front, Solid shading hides every bone inside the spheres and you cannot click them. With it, bones always draw on top, like an X-ray.

  2. Edit Mode: the Body bone, by numbers

    Hover the viewport, press Tab. Then the N sidebar › Item tab, which now shows Head and Tail.

    Do this:

    1. a
      With the armature selected (orange), hover the viewport and press Tab. The mode box (top-left) says Edit Mode and the header menus change to View, Select, Add, Armature, Bone.
    2. b
      Press N if the sidebar is closed. Its Item tab now shows the bone: Head X Y Z (the fat end) and Tail X Y Z (the thin tip).
    3. c
      Click Head Z, type 0.5, Enter. The fat end rises to just above the feet.
    4. d
      Click Tail Z, type 2, Enter. The tip now reaches the neck.
    5. e
      Hover the viewport, press F2, type Body, Enter.

    You should now see: one long bone up the middle of the penguin, from the top of the feet to the neck, and the sidebar name box reading Body.

    Why does the bone start at 0.5 and not 0?

    The feet and belly belong to this bone, but the fat end is where the bone pivots. Starting it a little way up keeps the pivot inside the body. The numbers were chosen so that automatic weights (Part 5) give each part to the right bone.

  3. Extrude the Head bone from the tip

    The viewport: the little ball at the TOP of Body.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the ball at the top of Body (its tail). Only that ball highlights.
    2. b
      Press E (extrude). A new bone grows out of the tip and follows your mouse.
    3. c
      Press Z, type 0.8, Enter. The new bone is exactly 0.8 m straight up.
    4. d
      F2, type Head, Enter.
    5. e
      Check the sidebar: Tail should read 0, 0, 2.8. If not, type those.

    You should now see: a second, shorter bone on top of Body, sharing the point at the neck. Head is a child of Body.

    Why extrude instead of Add?

    Extruding from a tip makes the new bone a connected child: it starts exactly where the parent ends and it will follow the parent. Add › Armature would make a separate skeleton that never moves with Body.

  4. Extrude Shoulder.L sideways

    The same neck ball, then E and X.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the ball at the neck again (where Body ends and Head starts). Blender extrudes from the tip of Body.
    2. b
      Press E, then X, type 0.6, Enter. A short bone points to screen-right: the penguin’s left.
    3. c
      F2, type Shoulder.L exactly (capital S, capital L, a dot), Enter.

    You should now see: a short horizontal bone from the neck out to the shoulder. Sidebar Tail: 0.6, 0, 2.

    Why a shoulder bone at all?

    If Arm.L grew straight out of the neck, it would pull the chest sphere with it when it waved and dent the body. The short shoulder bone takes the chest; the arm bone takes only the flipper. Try it without, as an extension, and watch the chest dent.

  5. The Arm.L bone, dropped then typed

    The tip of Shoulder.L, then the sidebar Tail boxes.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the tip ball of Shoulder.L (at the shoulder).
    2. b
      Press E, move the mouse down and out along the flipper, click to drop the new bone. Roughly is fine.
    3. c
      Sidebar: Tail X 1.15, Tail Z 0.9 (Y stays 0). The bone snaps into the flipper.
    4. d
      F2, type Arm.L, Enter. Press Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: four bones: Body, Head, Shoulder.L, Arm.L. The arm bone runs down the middle of the flipper from the shoulder to near its tip.

  6. Symmetrize: Blender builds the other side

    Viewport header › Armature menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport and press A so every bone is selected.
    2. b
      Armature › Symmetrize.
    3. c
      Look at the Outliner: expand Armature to see Shoulder.R and Arm.R under Body.

    You should now see: six bones, the right side a mirror of the left, with the new ones named Shoulder.R and Arm.R automatically.

    Why did the names matter?

    Symmetrize looks for names ending in .L, mirrors those bones across the X axis and names the copies .R. A bone called Shoulder (no .L) is ignored. If nothing happened, see Symmetrize did nothing.

  7. Test it in Pose Mode

    The mode box, or Ctrl+Tab. Then the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport, press Tab to leave Edit Mode, then Ctrl+Tab: Pose Mode. (Or pick Pose Mode from the mode box.) The bones turn grey-blue.
    2. b
      Click the Arm.L bone. It turns light blue.
    3. c
      Press R, Y, type -40, Enter. The bone swings out sideways. Nothing else moves yet: the penguin is not attached.
    4. d
      Press Alt+R to clear the rotation. Everything returns to rest.

    You should now see: the arm bone swinging and snapping back, with the penguin ignoring it completely.

    Why minus 40?

    In Front view, a positive rotation around Y turns the bone clockwise, which pushes this flipper into the body. Negative turns it out and up. The wave in Part 6 uses -110 for “flipper up”.

End of Part 4. Save.

Part 5

Attach the body to the skeleton

Tools: Select All by Type, Ctrl+P › With Automatic Weights.

Right now the bones and the spheres are strangers. One menu joins them: Blender looks at every sphere, finds the nearest bones, and glues each part to them. The order you select things decides who becomes the parent.

  1. Select the eight parts, then the armature last

    Viewport header › Select menu, then the Outliner.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport and press Ctrl+Tab to leave Pose Mode. The mode box must say Object Mode.
    2. b
      Select › Select All by Type › Mesh. All eight penguin parts turn orange. (The camera, light and drawings are not meshes, so they are left out.)
    3. c
      In the Outliner, hold Ctrl and click Armature. It joins the selection as the active object: a lighter orange than the others.

    You should now see: eight dark-orange wire eggs and a light-orange skeleton. The last thing you clicked is the parent-to-be.

    Why does the order matter?

    Ctrl+P always makes the ACTIVE object (the last one selected, drawn lighter) the parent of everything else selected. Click the armature first and you would parent the skeleton to a foot.

  2. Parent with automatic weights

    Mouse over the viewport. A pop-up menu appears under the mouse.

    Do this:

    1. a
      With the mouse over the viewport press Ctrl+P. The Set Parent To menu pops up.
    2. b
      Click With Automatic Weights (the indented line under Armature Deform).
    3. c
      Look at the Outliner: the eight parts are now listed under Armature, indented. Press Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: no change in the viewport, but the Outliner shows the parts as children of Armature.

    What are weights?

    Every vertex of every sphere now has a weight for each bone: how much that bone pulls it. Automatic Weights sets them by distance, so the flipper vertices belong to Arm.L and the belly vertices to Body. That is why the exact numbers mattered.

  3. Test: the penguin follows the bones

    The armature, Ctrl+Tab, then the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the skeleton (any bone) so Armature is active, then Ctrl+Tab: Pose Mode.
    2. b
      Click the Arm.L bone, press R Y, type -40, Enter. The flipper swings out WITH the bone.
    3. c
      Alt+R to clear it. Now click Body, press G and move the mouse: the whole penguin walks. Alt+G puts it back.
    4. d
      Press Ctrl+S. Switch to Solid shading (Shift+Z) to see the penguin as a solid shape while it bends.

    You should now see: the flipper mesh bending with its bone, and the whole penguin moving with Body.

    Why does moving Body move everything?

    Body is the top of the family tree, so every other bone follows it, and every sphere follows its bones. That is the whole point of a skeleton: one handle for the whole character.

End of Part 5. Save.

Part 6

Animate the wave

Tools: the Timeline, I (insert keyframe), Space (play).

Animation is a list of poses at chosen frames. You will set five: rest, flipper up, part-way down, up again, rest. Blender works out every frame in between. Try it below before you do it in Blender.

Keyframe explorer

Five keyframes (the yellow diamonds) and the 43 frames Blender fills in. Drag the frame slider or press Play.

  1. Make the animation 2 seconds long

    The Timeline: the strip along the bottom of the window. Its header has the play buttons and the Start and End boxes.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Find the Timeline at the bottom. If it is too thin to read, drag its top edge upwards.
    2. b
      Click the End box, type 48, Enter. Leave Start at 1.

    You should now see: the Timeline ruler running from 1 to 48.

    Why 48?

    Blender plays 24 frames every second by default, like a cinema film. 48 frames is two seconds, long enough for one wave, and short enough that you will not get lost.

  2. Keyframe the rest pose at frame 1

    Pose Mode, the viewport, and the Timeline.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Pose Mode (click the skeleton, Ctrl+Tab). The blue marker in the Timeline must be at frame 1: if not, press Shift+←.
    2. b
      Hover the viewport, press A: all bones selected.
    3. c
      Press I (the letter i). That records every bone’s pose on frame 1.

    You should now see: a yellow diamond at frame 1 in the Timeline, and the sidebar boxes turned yellow.

    Why key everything at frame 1?

    A keyframe only stores the bones that were selected. Keying all of them at rest means every bone has a starting pose, so nothing drifts, and the loop ends exactly where it began.

  3. Frame 12: flipper up

    The current-frame box in the Timeline header, then the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the current-frame box (it shows 1), type 12, Enter. The blue marker jumps to 12.
    2. b
      Click the Arm.L bone so it is the only one selected.
    3. c
      Press R Y, type -110, Enter. The flipper swings right up. The sidebar Rotation boxes turn orange: changed, not saved.
    4. d
      Press I. The boxes turn yellow and a diamond appears at 12.

    You should now see: a second diamond at frame 12. Drag the blue marker between 1 and 12: the flipper rises on its own.

    Why change the frame first?

    A keyframe lands on whatever frame the marker is on. Pose first, then move the marker, and the pose you made is thrown away when the frame changes. Frame, pose, I. Always in that order.

  4. Frames 24, 36 and 48

    Same three places: frame box, viewport, I.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Frame box 24, Enter. Arm.L still selected: R Y 40 Enter (it drops part-way). Press I.
    2. b
      Frame box 36, Enter. R Y -40 Enter (back up). Press I.
    3. c
      Frame box 48, Enter. Alt+R (rest pose, the same as frame 1, so the loop joins up). Press I.

    You should now see: five diamonds: 1, 12, 24, 36, 48.

    Why 40 at frame 24 but -110 at frame 12?

    R adds to the current pose. At frame 12 the flipper went from 0 to -110. At frame 24, adding 40 takes it from -110 to -70: part-way down. At 36, -40 takes it back to -110. Alt+R at 48 returns it to 0.

  5. Play it

    The viewport (mouse over it) and the Timeline.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Press Shift+← to jump to frame 1.
    2. b
      Hover the viewport and press Space. The marker sweeps along and the flipper waves, over and over. Space again stops it.
    3. c
      Press Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: a waving penguin. If the flipper goes up but not down, or something else moves, see the flipper does not move.

    What is Blender doing between the keys?

    For every frame without a diamond it blends the nearest keys, easing out of one and into the next (Bezier). Switch the Keyframe explorer above to Linear to see the difference: a robot wave.

  6. Save and hand in

    Ctrl+S, then SEQTA.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Ctrl+S. The bottom bar flashes Saved.
    2. b
      Upload Lab10_Penguin_YourName.blend to SEQTA under Lab 10. The .blend file itself, not a screenshot.

    You should now see: your file in SEQTA.

End of the lab.

Part 7

Finished early? Pick one

Tools: Materials, more keyframes, more bones, the camera and rendering.

Each block below is a small project on its own. Do them in any order; A (colours) is the quickest win and E (the movie) is the best thing to hand in. Every step is laid out like the main lab: where to look, an animation, and the moves.

A. Give it colours (3 steps, 10 minutes)

A material is the recipe for how a surface looks. You make two, black and orange, and share them between parts.

  1. The first material: a black belly

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the red sphere tab, Material. Object Mode.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Hover the viewport and press Shift+Z so the shading is Solid (the drawings get in the way of colours; you can hide the two Empties in the Outliner with their eye icons).
    2. b
      Click the Belly. In the Properties editor click the red sphere tab: Material.
    3. c
      Click New. A material called Material appears, with a Base Color row under Surface.
    4. d
      Click the white Base Color swatch. A colour picker pops up. Click its Hex tab, type 1A1A1A, press Enter.
    5. e
      Double-click the name box (it says Material) and type Black so you can find it again.

    You should now see: a black belly, and a material called Black in the slot list.

    Why Hex?

    A hex code is six characters that name an exact colour, the same way web pages do. 1A1A1A is a very dark grey that reads as black but still shows shading. 000000 would be a flat black hole.

  2. Share the black with four more parts

    The viewport (Object Mode) and the Object menu in its header.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click Chest. Hold Shift and click Head, Arm.L and Arm.R.
    2. b
      Still holding Shift, click the Belly last. It is now the active object (brighter orange), and it is the one that has the material.
    3. c
      Object › Link/Transfer Data › Link Materials. (Shortcut: Ctrl+L, then Link Materials.)

    You should now see: five black parts. Click any of them: the Material tab shows the same Black material.

    Why link instead of making five materials?

    One material shared by five objects means one change recolours all five. It is also how real studios work: a few materials, many objects.

  3. Orange beak and feet, then look at it

    Material tab again, then the Object menu, then the shading pie menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Beak. Material tab › New › Base Color › Hex FF7A14 › Enter. Name it Orange.
    2. b
      Click Foot.L, Shift-click Foot.R, Shift-click the Beak last. Object › Link/Transfer Data › Link Materials.
    3. c
      Hover the viewport, press Z and click Material Preview in the pie that appears. (Shift+Z brings Wireframe back whenever you want it.)

    You should now see: a black penguin with an orange beak and orange feet, lit and shiny in the viewport.

    Why Material Preview?

    Solid shading ignores materials and shows every object grey. Material Preview is a quick render in the viewport. Rendered is the full render; slower, but it shows the lights too.

B. White tummy and eyes (2 steps, 10 minutes)

Three more spheres. The important part is the end: anything added after Part 5 has to be attached to the skeleton again or it stays behind when the penguin moves.

  1. The tummy

    Add menu, the sidebar, the Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. Sidebar: Location X 0, Y -0.55, Z 1.05. Scale X 0.55, Y 0.3, Z 0.6.
    2. b
      Material tab › New › Hex F2F2F2. Name it White. F2, type Tummy, Enter.

    You should now see: a white dome on the front of the belly. In Right view it pokes out toward -Y, the front.

    Why -0.55?

    The belly is 0.75 deep (Scale Y), so its front surface is at Y -0.75. A sphere centred at -0.55 with depth 0.3 reaches out to -0.85: 10 cm proud of the belly, like a real tummy patch.

  2. Two eyes, then attach all three to the skeleton

    Add, the sidebar, then the Outliner and Ctrl+P over the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. Location X 0.17, Y -0.38, Z 2.55. Scale 0.06, 0.06, 0.06. Click Tummy, Shift-click the eye, Ctrl+L › Link Materials (white). F2: Eye.L.
    2. b
      With Eye.L selected: Shift+D, then X, type -0.34, Enter. F2: Eye.R.
    3. c
      Click Tummy, Shift-click Eye.L and Eye.R. In the Outliner hold Ctrl and click Armature so it is active.
    4. d
      Hover the viewport, Ctrl+P › With Automatic Weights, exactly like Step 24.

    You should now see: Tummy, Eye.L and Eye.R listed under Armature in the Outliner. Pose Mode: bend Body and the eyes come along.

    Why attach again?

    Step 24 only weighted the eight parts that existed then. New objects know nothing about the bones until you parent them. Forget this and the eyes hover in mid-air while the penguin bows.

C. Make it at least 100 frames (2 steps, 15 minutes)

Two more waves and a bow. Same recipe as Part 6: frame, pose, I.

  1. A second wave: frames 48 to 96

    Timeline End box, then Pose Mode with Arm.L selected.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: End 96. Pose Mode, click the Arm.L bone.
    2. b
      Frame 60: R Y -110, I. Frame 72: R Y 40, I.
    3. c
      Frame 84: R Y -40, I. Frame 96: Alt+R, I.
    4. d
      Shift+←, Space: two waves in a row, four seconds.

    You should now see: nine diamonds in the Timeline when Arm.L is selected, and a penguin that waves twice.

    Why not copy the keys?

    You can: in the Timeline, select the diamonds at 12, 24, 36, 48, press Shift+D and drag them 48 frames right. Typing them again is slower but shows you that a wave is just four poses.

  2. A bow with the Body bone

    Right view (red X circle), Pose Mode, the Body bone.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the red X circle on the gizmo: Right view. Click the Body bone. Frame 48: press I (upright, keyed).
    2. b
      Frame 56: R X 20, Enter. The whole penguin tips forward, flippers and all. Press I.
    3. c
      Frame 64: Alt+R, I. Play from 48: a quick bow before the second wave.

    You should now see: the beak dipping and the back rising at frame 56, then upright again at 64.

    Why X this time?

    In Right view you are looking along the X axis, so rotating around X is the only way to tip something toward or away from you. Y would make the penguin lean sideways; Z would spin it like a top.

D. Leg bones (2 steps, 15 minutes, harder)

Two bones per leg, grown from the bottom of Body. One catch: a bone grown from a head is not connected to anything, so you parent it yourself.

  1. Grow and attach the left leg, then mirror it

    Edit Mode of the armature; the sidebar Tail boxes; the Armature menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the armature, Tab for Edit Mode. Click the ball at the bottom of Body (its head, 0.5 m up).
    2. b
      E, X, type 0.35, Enter: a hip bone out to the side. F2: Hip.L.
    3. c
      E, Z, type -0.35, Enter: a leg bone down into the foot. F2: Leg.L.
    4. d
      Click Hip.L, Shift-click Body, Ctrl+P › Keep Offset. Now Hip.L is Body’s child (a dotted line joins them).
    5. e
      A, then Armature › Symmetrize. Hip.R and Leg.R appear.

    You should now see: ten bones. In the Outliner, expand Armature: Hip.L sits under Body, Leg.L under Hip.L, and the same on the right.

    Why Keep Offset and not Connected?

    Connected would drag Hip.L’s head onto Body’s tail at the neck. Keep Offset leaves it at the hip and just makes Body the parent, which is what a hip joint needs.

  2. Re-weight the body to the new bones

    Object Mode; the Select menu, the Outliner, and Ctrl+P.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Tab to leave Edit Mode. Select › Select All by Type › Mesh.
    2. b
      In the Outliner hold Ctrl and click Armature.
    3. c
      Hover the viewport, Ctrl+P › With Automatic Weights. Blender recalculates every weight; the feet now belong to the legs.
    4. d
      Test: Pose Mode, click Leg.L, R Y 30: a foot lifts. Alt+R.

    You should now see: a foot that lifts when its leg bone turns, and a belly that stays put.

    What about the old keyframes?

    They are still there: Arm.L keeps its wave and Body its bow. New bones simply have no keys yet. Key a little walk at frames 100 onwards if you like.

E. Point a camera at it and render the movie (2 steps, 15 minutes + render time)

The movie is what you will show people. The camera gets exact numbers like everything else, then Blender renders every frame into one .mp4.

  1. Place the camera

    The Outliner, the sidebar Item tab, and Numpad 0.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click Camera in the Outliner. The sidebar now shows the camera’s numbers (press N if the sidebar is closed).
    2. b
      Location X 6, Y -7, Z 3.2. Rotation X 80, Y 0, Z 40.
    3. c
      Hover the viewport and press Numpad 0: you look through the camera. The penguin should fill the middle of the frame. Numpad 0 again goes back.

    You should now see: the penguin seen from its front-right, waving at the camera, inside the dotted camera frame.

    Where do the numbers come from?

    Rotation Z 40 turns the camera to face the penguin from that corner; X 80 tilts it 10 degrees below level so it looks slightly down. Change X by 5 and watch the horizon move.

  2. Render the movie

    Properties editor › the printer tab, Output. Then the Render menu at the very top.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the printer tab: Output. Under Format, set Resolution % to 50 so each frame renders in seconds.
    2. b
      Under Output: File Format › FFmpeg Video. An Encoding panel appears: Container › MPEG-4.
    3. c
      Click the folder icon in the Output path box and pick your Lab 10 folder.
    4. d
      Render › Render Animation (Ctrl+F12). A window shows every frame rendering. Leave it until it stops.
    5. e
      Find 0001-0048.mp4 (or 0001-0096) in your folder and double-click it. Upload it to SEQTA with the .blend.

    You should now see: a movie file in your Lab 10 folder that plays in any player.

    Why FFmpeg and MPEG-4?

    PNG, the default, would give you 48 separate pictures. FFmpeg Video joins them into one file, and MPEG-4 (.mp4) is the format every phone, laptop and SEQTA upload understands.

Something’s not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

I pressed X and something vanished

X is delete. Press Ctrl+Z until it comes back (Blender remembers 32 steps). For views use the gizmo circles or the numpad.

I added the drawing but can’t see it

Three usual causes. 1) You were not in Front (or Right) view when you added it, so it faces the wrong way: delete the Empty in the Outliner and redo the step from the gizmo click. 2) It is huge: 5 m. Scroll the mouse wheel to zoom out. 3) It is there but the viewport is in Solid shading and a sphere covers it: press Shift+Z.

The beak points the wrong way in Right view

You added penguin_front.png in the side view (or the other way round). Click the drawing’s orange outline, press X, Delete, and redo Step 5 with penguin_side.png.

I can’t orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured gizmo itself to orbit. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

I added a sphere but can’t find it

It appeared at the 3D cursor, inside the belly. Look at the Outliner: a new Sphere row is highlighted. Just type the sidebar numbers and it moves into place. If the cursor is somewhere odd, press Shift+C before adding the next one.

I typed Scale numbers but it moved, or it grew instead of moving

You typed into the wrong row. The sidebar has three groups: Location (metres), Rotation (degrees) and Scale (no unit). Press Ctrl+Z and find the right box. If a number shows as 0.95 m instead of 0.95, that is the same thing.

Shift+D moved my original, or I have two spheres in one place

Shift+D makes the copy and starts moving it. If you clicked before typing X -1.9, the copy was dropped on top of the original. Click it (it is the one that is selected), then press G X -1.9 Enter. If you pressed D twice you have three; delete the extra one with X.

The menus are different from the lab, or keys do nothing

Check the mode box at the top-left of the viewport. Object Mode for Parts 1–3 and Step 23–24; Edit Mode for Steps 17–21; Pose Mode for Steps 22 and 25–30. Tab toggles Edit, Ctrl+Tab toggles Pose. Also make sure the right object is active (highlighted in the Outliner): the armature for bone work.

E made a bone in the wrong place, or a floating bone

Press Esc during the move, or Ctrl+Z after it. Make sure you clicked the small ball at the TIP, not the body of the bone: clicking the body selects the whole bone and E then extrudes from its tip anyway, which is fine, but clicking the fat end extrudes a bone that is not connected. Whatever happened, the sidebar Tail numbers fix the position.

Symmetrize did nothing

Three checks: you are in Edit Mode of the armature (not Object or Pose); every bone is selected (press A); the names end in .L exactly: Shoulder.L and Arm.L, capital L, a full stop. Shoulder_L and shoulder.l do not count. Fix the names with F2 and run Symmetrize again.

Ctrl+Tab opens a wheel of modes instead of switching

That is the pie menu some setups show. Just click Pose Mode in it. Or ignore the shortcut and choose Pose Mode from the mode box at the top-left of the viewport.

Ctrl+P does not show “With Automatic Weights”

The armature is not the active object. Redo Step 23: parts first (Select › Select All by Type › Mesh), then Ctrl+click Armature in the Outliner so it is the lighter orange. The mouse must be over the viewport when you press Ctrl+P.

The bone moves but the penguin does not

Parenting did not happen or missed some parts. In the Outliner the eight parts must be nested under Armature. If any are not: Object Mode, select the loose parts, Ctrl+click Armature, Ctrl+P › With Automatic Weights.

Everything moves when I rotate the arm

More than one bone is selected, probably all of them from Step 27. In Pose Mode click empty space (or Alt+A) to deselect, then click only the Arm.L bone. The viewport text next to the frame number shows which bone is active.

When I press Space the flipper does not move, or only goes up

Look at the diamonds in the Timeline with Arm.L selected: there should be five. A missing diamond means you moved the frame before pressing I; go to that frame, pose it again, press I. If the flipper is up at every frame, the first key at frame 1 was made after you posed it: go to frame 1, Alt+R, I. Also check End is 48, not 250.

The sidebar boxes are orange

Orange means changed but not keyed. Press I while the bone is selected. If you did not mean to change anything, Alt+R then I.

The drawings have gone pink

Blender cannot find the PNG files any more because they were moved or renamed. Put them back next to the .blend, or add them again with Steps 4–5.

I gave it a colour but everything is still grey

The viewport is in Solid shading, which ignores materials. Hover the viewport, press Z and choose Material Preview. (Shift+Z toggles Wireframe; Z opens the full shading menu.)

The tummy or eyes stay behind when the penguin moves

They were added after the parenting in Step 24, so the skeleton does not know about them. Select them, Ctrl+click Armature in the Outliner, then Ctrl+P › With Automatic Weights (Step E5).

The chest dents or stretches when the flipper waves

Automatic weights gave part of the chest to Arm.L. Usually because the chest or flipper numbers were not typed exactly (compare with the table in Part 2) or the Shoulder.L bone was skipped. Fix the numbers, then redo Steps 23–24: Blender recalculates the weights.

Eight quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You’ll find out straight away whether you’re right.

1In Blender, what does the X key do when a sphere is selected?

Right. X deletes. The views come from the gizmo or the numpad.

Not quite. X deletes whatever is selected. Views are the gizmo or the numpad; X only locks an axis if you press G, R or S first.

2You press G, then Z, then move the mouse. What happens?

Right. G is grab; the Z straight after locks it to the Z axis.

Not quite. G moves; pressing Z after it locks the move to up-and-down.

3In Front view, where is the penguin’s LEFT flipper?

Right. The penguin faces you, so its left is on your right, the +X side. That is why the bone is Arm.L.

Not quite. The penguin faces you, so its left is your right: the +X side, where Arm.L is.

4Why must the bones be named Shoulder.L and Arm.L before Step 21?

Right. Symmetrize mirrors .L bones and names the copies .R.

Not quite. The .L ending is what Symmetrize looks for; it mirrors those bones and names the copies .R.

5To grow a connected child bone, which end do you click before pressing E?

Right. Extruding from the tail makes a child that starts exactly where the parent ends.

Not quite. Click the thin tip (tail). Extruding from the fat end gives a bone that is not connected.

6Before Ctrl+P, which object must be selected LAST?

Right. The last one clicked is the active object, and Ctrl+P makes the active object the parent.

Not quite. The armature must be active (clicked last, lighter orange) so that it becomes the parent.

7A sidebar box has turned yellow. What does that mean?

Right. Yellow is a key on this frame; green is animated elsewhere; orange is changed and unsaved.

Not quite. Yellow = keyframe on this frame. Green = animated but no key here. Orange = changed, press I.

8The Timeline runs 1 to 48 at 24 frames per second. How long is the animation?

Right. 48 ÷ 24 = 2 seconds.

Not quite. 24 frames is one second, so 48 frames is two.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

Which single number, if you got it wrong, would do the most damage later in the lab, and why? If you wanted the penguin to nod its head instead of wave, which bone would you key, and with which key presses?

Upload to SEQTA — Lab 10

Upload Lab10_Penguin_YourName.blend. It should contain the two drawings, the eight named parts, the six-bone armature with the parts parented to it, and the five keyframes on Arm.L.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

About three lessons. Lesson 1: Parts 1–3 (the drawings and the eight spheres; the numbers table lets fast students race ahead). Lesson 2: Parts 4–5 (the skeleton and parenting; this is where the old version lost people). Lesson 3: Part 6, the quiz and extensions.

What changed from the previous version of this lab

  • The reference pictures are now provided (download buttons in Step 2). The old sheet said “picture provided” but shipped none, and every number here depends on these exact drawings (5 m square, feet 1.45 m below the centre).
  • Views by gizmo or numpad, never letters. The old steps said “press -y” and “press X” for views. X deletes. Students followed it literally.
  • Every sphere has exact Location/Rotation/Scale values (table in Part 2) instead of “G + S to resize”. G and S are still taught in Step 7 as the rough first pass. “Edit view” and “click in front” are now the real names: Edit Mode, and Armature Data › Viewport Display › In Front.
  • The mirror step is explicit: Shift+D, X -1.9, R Y 50. The duplicated Step 14 in the old sheet is gone.
  • Bones are built from the tip with E and typed numbers; the old “click the edge of the bone” is now “click the ball at the tail”. Shoulder bones were added so the chest does not dent when the flipper waves (verified in the renders).
  • One parenting step for all eight parts (Select All by Type › Mesh, Ctrl+click Armature, Ctrl+P › With Automatic Weights) replaces parenting each part separately, and the active-object rule is explained.
  • The animation part is new: the old sheet stopped at “animate it”. Five keyframes, the frame-then-pose-then-I order, the yellow/green/orange colours, and Alt+R for a clean loop.
  • The extensions are now full steps (E1–E11, Part 7) with the same Where / Watch / Do-this layout: materials and Link Materials, tummy and eyes with the re-parenting trap, a 96-frame double wave and a bow, leg bones with Keep Offset, and a camera plus an MP4 render. Their ticks are saved but not counted in the 31.
  • The follow-on sheet (old Labs 14–15) suggested a YouTube-to-MP3 converter for soundtracks. That is left out; if you want sound, use a licence-free track from the school library.

Tested values

Every number, menu path and shortcut was checked in Blender 4.2 LTS (4.2.23). The checkpoint pictures were rendered from a file built by exactly these steps, including the automatic weights and the five keyframes. Menu names also match Blender 4.x onwards. The pose-mode sidebar shows quaternion rotation (W X Y Z); students are told to ignore it and use R Y. The “Ctrl+Tab shows a pie menu” case is covered in the troubleshooting.

Where students usually get stuck

Adding a reference image while not in a front or side view (it then faces the wrong way). Typing into the Location row when the step says Scale. Clicking the armature first instead of last before Ctrl+P (the skeleton becomes a child of a foot). Posing before changing the frame, so the pose is lost. Having every bone selected from Step 27 when rotating the arm in Step 28, so the whole penguin spins.

Quiz answers

1 Deletes. 2 Moves only up and down. 3 On the right of the screen (+X). 4 Symmetrize only mirrors .L bones. 5 The thin tip. 6 The armature. 7 A keyframe on this frame. 8 Two seconds.

Quick rubric

CriterionDevelopingAchievedExtending
ModelSome spheres, not matching the drawingsEight parts matching both drawings, named correctlyTummy, eyes or colours added and attached to the rig
SkeletonBones present but floating or misnamedSix bones with correct heads, tails and names; Symmetrize usedLeg bones added and weighted, or a second character rigged
RigSome parts do not follow the bonesAll parts parented with automatic weights; chest keeps its shapeWeights adjusted by hand where needed
AnimationKeys missing; the loop jumpsFive keys, smooth wave, End 48, loops cleanly100+ frames with a second move (bow or nod) that reads clearly, or an MP4 render
